title: Celebrating the birth of new stars... and the VST!
caption: The nebulae Gum 10 and Gum 11, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Red-orange clouds sprawl across this picture, streaked with black lines. The bright cloud that dominates is Gum 10, and the fainter, separate cloud at the bottom left is Gum 11. Some viewers may see a chicken pecking at seeds, or the head of a dragon.

The pair belong to a larger complex where stars are born, visible mostly from the southern hemisphere. Hot, massive stars in each nebula give off ultraviolet light strong enough to tear electrons away from hydrogen atoms. When the electrons later rejoin the hydrogen ions, they give off the particular shade of red. The black lines are dust blocking the light behind it.

The picture was released on the fifteenth anniversary of first light for the VLT Survey Telescope, which took it. The data come from VPHAS+, a project scanning the plane of the Milky Way to better understand the life cycle of stars.

understand.summary: The VLT Survey Telescope took this visible-light image. The filters and colour mapping aren't published.
understand.eye: The camera builds up a red glow from hydrogen over long exposures, far brighter than the eye would see it.

explore: The VST began as a joint project between ESO and the Capodimonte Astronomical Observatory, which belongs to INAF, Italy's national astrophysics institute. Today INAF manages it alone, and ESO hosts it at Paranal Observatory in Chile.
alt: Large red-orange clouds with black dust lanes, and a smaller detached cloud at bottom left.
